claims.text: The component alloy is susceptible to hot cracking during fusion-welding repair.
Cold spray deposition can be used to apply a repair layer to the damaged region.
A low-temperature post-deposition heat treatment can promote interfacial bonding without melting the alloy.
An inert processing atmosphere prevents oxidation during the repair.
Cold spray can provide high particle velocity while keeping the deposited material below its melting temperature.
Cold spray produces a refined interfacial microstructure.
The cold-sprayed repair avoids fusion-induced residual stress and cracking.
The deposited layer develops strong mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding with the substrate.
Cold spray deposition bonds particles through high-velocity impact and plastic deformation rather than melting.
Avoiding melting also avoids the thermal cycles that trigger hot cracking in the alloy.
Low-temperature post-treatment causes controlled interdiffusion at the repair interface.
Controlled interdiffusion strengthens the interfacial bond without altering the beneficial microstructure.
Cold-spray repair will produce less hot cracking than traditional fusion-welding repair.
Cold-spray repair will provide improved or maintained bond strength relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
Cold-spray repair will provide greater durability under aggressive cyclic thermal and mechanical service than traditional fusion-welding repair.
Traditional fusion welding is prone to inducing hot cracking in the heat-sensitive alloy.
Keeping repair temperatures significantly below the melting point avoids microstructural degradation.
